name: Great Bentley
text: Your train passes Great Bentley, on the train's {side}, a village scattered round a 43-acre green, the second largest village green in the United Kingdom. The name probably comes from bent, a kind of grass, and ley, land sown with grass: a reference to the green itself.

name: Weeley
text: Your train passes near Weeley, on the train's {side}, which during the Napoleonic Wars had barracks for up to 3,000 men, at first from three Scottish Highland battalions; the garrisons of the Martello towers along the coast were based here. In August 1971 it hosted the Weeley Festival.

name: Vista Road Recreation Ground
text: Your train passes near Vista Road Recreation Ground, on the train's {side}, where Essex played 60 first-class cricket matches between 1931, against Lancashire, and 1966, against Leicestershire. Clacton Cricket Club plays there today.

name: Thorpe Hall gardens
text: Your train passes near the gardens of Thorpe Hall, on the train's {side}, laid out by Evelyn Byng after her husband, Julian Byng, 1st Viscount Byng of Vimy, bought the estate in 1913. He died there in 1935; the Georgian manor house was later demolished and replaced by a spa.

name: Frinton-on-Sea
text: Your train passes Frinton-on-Sea, on the train's {side}, a village said to have just six houses in the early 1870s that was laid out as a resort from the 1880s; its station opened in 1888. The industrialist Richard Powell Cooper banned boarding houses and pubs, and the town's first pub, the Lock and Barrel, opened only in 2000.

name: Frinton Park Estate
text: Your train passes near Frinton Park Estate, on the train's {side}, planned in 1934 with 1,100 houses and a showcase of modern architecture overseen by Oliver Hill. The public was wary of experimental housing, and only about 40 modernist houses were built; after the Second World War the rest of the estate was built in a conventional way.

name: Mistley Towers
text: Your train passes near Mistley Towers, on the train's {side}, the twin towers of a church that Robert Adam was asked in 1776 to make grander for Richard Rigby, who hoped to turn Mistley into a spa town. The nave was pulled down around 1870, leaving only the two towers standing.

name: Bradfield
text: Your train passes near Bradfield, on the train's {side}, a village of Anglo-Saxon origin whose Old English name, Bradefelda, means a broad stretch of open land. No Roman settlement has been found here, but pieces of Roman brick and tile are built into St Lawrence's church.

name: Copperas Wood
text: Your train passes near Copperas Wood, on the train's {side}, an Essex Wildlife Trust reserve of ancient sweet chestnut and hornbeam coppice. Around 100 kinds of bird have been seen here, and more than 300 of moths; the Great Storm of 1987 left some areas to grow back naturally.

name: Harwich International Port
text: Your train passes near Harwich International Port, on the train's {side}, built by the Great Eastern Railway on reclaimed land and opened in 1883 as Parkeston Quay, named after the company's chairman, Charles Parkes. In December 1938 young Jewish refugees of the Kindertransport arrived here.

name: Harwich Redoubt
text: Your train passes near Harwich Redoubt, on the train's {side}, a circular brick fort built from 1808 to 1810 against a Napoleonic invasion. From its hilltop its guns could fire across the mouths of the Stour and the Orwell, alongside those of Landguard Fort on the far shore.

name: Sir Bobby Robson Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Sir Bobby Robson Bridge, on the train's {side}, a cable-stayed footbridge over the River Gipping, built in 2009 and named after the former Ipswich Town and England manager. It's the second highest structure in Ipswich.

name: Clifford Road Tunnels
text: Your train passes near the Clifford Road Tunnels, on the train's {side}, an air-raid shelter for 200 people dug under a school playground early in the Second World War. Long thought to have been filled in, it was found again in 1989 when workmen digging a pond came upon one of its stairways, and it's now a museum of the home front.

name: Ipswich Transport Museum
text: Your train passes near Ipswich Transport Museum, on the train's {side}, in the old Priory Heath trolleybus depot. Its collection of more than 100 large objects includes trams, trolleybuses and buses from Ipswich, fire engines, cranes and prams.

name: Trimley St Mary
text: Your train passes near Trimley St Mary, on the train's {side}, a village famous, with its neighbour Trimley St Martin, for two parish churches standing side by side in one churchyard. They are said to have been built as the result of a family feud.

name: Playford Hall
text: Your train passes near Playford Hall, on the train's {side}, where Thomas Clarkson, the campaigner against the slave trade, lived from 1816 until his death in 1846; he's buried in the village churchyard.

name: Woodbridge Tide Mill
text: Your train passes near Woodbridge Tide Mill, on the train's {side}, one of the few tide mills whose wheel still turns and can grind flour. A mill has stood here since at least 1170; this one, from the 17th century, was the last tide mill working commercially in Britain when it closed in 1957.

name: Campsey Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Campsey Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Augustinian canonesses founded shortly before 1195 by Theobald de Valoines for two of his sisters. It was suppressed in 1536; the site is now a private house.

name: Beversham
text: Your train passes near Beversham, on the train's {side}, a place with two households in the Domesday Book, of which little now remains. Its early 19th-century watermill, derelict in 1975, has since been restored, and the level crossing here dates from the line's opening in 1859.

name: Cockfield Hall
text: Your train passes near the park of Cockfield Hall, on the train's {side}, a Grade I house thought to have been built in its Tudor brick form by Sir Arthur Hopton, perhaps around 1520. In 1567 Queen Elizabeth I ordered his son, Sir Owen Hopton, to hold Lady Catherine Grey, sister of Lady Jane Grey, here.

name: St Andrew's Church, Bramfield
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church at Bramfield, on the train's {side}, whose round tower, from the 12th century, stands apart from the church. It's the only detached round tower in Suffolk, and both church and tower are Grade I listed.

name: RAF Halesworth
text: Your train passes near the site of RAF Halesworth, on the train's {side}, an airfield built in 1942 and 1943 as a bomber station. Its first users were the American 56th Fighter Group, who arrived in July 1943 with P-47 Thunderbolts and produced many of the Eighth Air Force's top fighter aces.

name: Beccles bell tower
text: Your train passes near the bell tower of St Michael's Church in Beccles, on the train's {side}, which stands apart from the church near a cliff above the River Waveney. Building began around 1500, and 122 steps lead to views as far as the North Sea.

name: Castle Marshes
text: Your train passes near Castle Marshes, on the train's {side}, a Suffolk Wildlife Trust reserve of fen and grazing marsh west of Lowestoft. The nationally rare Norfolk hawker dragonfly breeds here, and in winter, when the marshes flood, migrant birds join the resident wigeons, teals and shovelers.

name: Oulton Broad
text: Your train passes near Oulton Broad, on the train's {side}, the most southerly stretch of open water in the Broads, believed to be left from medieval peat digging. Mutford Lock joins it to the salt water of Lake Lothing, and Oulton Dyke to the River Waveney.

name: South Broads Lifeboat Station
text: Your train passes near the former South Broads Lifeboat Station, on the train's {side}, set up by the RNLI in 2001 to try out lifeboats on inland waters. It covered the southern Broads and the River Waveney, and made 194 rescues before closing in 2011.

name: Somerleyton Swing Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Waveney, and the border between Suffolk and Norfolk, on Somerleyton Swing Bridge, built in 1905 to carry two tracks in place of a single-track bridge. It's one of only four railway swing bridges still crossing rivers in the Broads.

name: Reedham Swing Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Yare on Reedham Swing Bridge, built in 1902 and 1903 on the site of a Victorian bridge that let tall wherry boats through. It's worked from its own signal box of 1904, and in a typical year it opens about 1,300 times.

name: Cantley
text: Your train passes Cantley, on the train's {side}, home of a sugar factory founded in 1912 by a Dutch company, using machinery shipped from a closed factory in Dordrecht. It closed in 1916 and reopened in 1920; today British Sugar runs it, one of four sugar factories in Britain.

name: Buckenham Marshes
text: Your train runs along Buckenham Marshes, on the train's {side}, an RSPB reserve beside the River Yare and the only place in England where bean geese regularly spend the winter. Up to 80,000 rooks roost here, in the largest rookery in Britain.

name: Strumpshaw Fen
text: Your train passes Strumpshaw Fen, on the train's {side}, an RSPB reserve on the River Yare since 1974. It's one of the few places in Great Britain where the swallowtail butterfly breeds, and in spring you may hear the booming of bitterns.

name: Brundall signal box
text: Your train passes Brundall signal box, on the train's {side}, a Great Eastern Railway box listed in 2013 as one of 26 “highly distinctive” signal boxes. Control moved to Colchester in 2020, and the box is to be preserved on the Mid-Norfolk Railway.

name: Carrow Road
text: Your train passes near Carrow Road, on the train's {side}, home of Norwich City, built in just 82 days and opened in August 1935. Its biggest crowd, 43,984, came in 1963 for an FA Cup match against Leicester City, when fans could still stand on the terraces.

name: Trowse Swing Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Wensum on Trowse Swing Bridge, the third bridge here since George Parker Bidder built the first in 1845. Today's single-track bridge was put in during the winter of 1986 and 1987, after being trial-erected in a workshop in Derbyshire.

name: Wymondham Bridewell
text: Your train passes near Wymondham Bridewell, on the train's {side}, the town's prison from as early as 1619. The present building, from the 1780s, had 22 cells and a treadmill; it closed as a prison in 1878, and now houses Wymondham Heritage Museum.

name: Spooner Row
text: Your train passes Spooner Row, on the train's {side}, a small village that was part of the parish of Wymondham until 2019. Its station is a request stop, with only a handful of trains and none on Sundays.

name: Attleborough church
text: Your train passes near Attleborough's parish church, on the train's {side}, partly Norman and partly 14th century. Its rood screen, with the loft above it intact for its full width, is one of the finest in Norfolk.

name: The English Distillery
text: Your train passes near the English Distillery, on the train's {side}, which in 2006 became the first distillery in England built for single malt whisky in 100 years. Its barley comes from Norfolk, where it would once have gone to Scotland's whisky makers.

name: St Andrew's Church, Roudham
text: Your train passes near the ruins of St Andrew's Church at Roudham, on the train's {side}, abandoned after a fire in 1736. Its walls still stand to their full height, though the building is so weak it has had to be fenced off.

name: Thetford Priory
text: Your train passes near Thetford Priory, on the train's {side}, a Cluniac monastery founded in 1103 by Roger Bigod and one of the most important in East Anglia. It held the tombs of the Howard family and of Henry FitzRoy, Duke of Richmond and Somerset; when it closed in 1540, the Howard tombs were moved to Framlingham.
